notes: The question holds together God’s presence among human beings and the impossibility of containing God in a building.
The oath belongs to a dispute between neighbors. The prayer asks God to distinguish guilt from innocence; it does not describe the procedure in detail.
The foreigner is explicitly someone outside Israel. The request extends hearing and response to that person’s prayer.
The Hebrew can mean the faithful love shown to David or David’s own acts of loyalty. Fluent follows the first possibility.
vocabulary: Berit and hesed join pledged relationship with enduring loyalty.
These paired requests recur throughout the prayer, connecting its different situations.
Teshuah means deliverance or rescue; here it is pictured as clothing.

notes: The account distinguishes seven days for the altar dedication, seven for the festival, and the closing assembly. It dates the departure to the twenty-third day.
The promise answers Solomon’s temple prayer and addresses the people who bear God’s name in their land.
The Hebrew shifts from addressing you all to speaking of them. The draft preserves that shift.
vocabulary: Hesed repeats the thanksgiving refrain from 5:13 and 1 Chronicles 16.
Kana describes yielding or lowering oneself; it recurs in Rehoboam’s response in chapter 12.

notes: Here Huram gives towns to Solomon. The different direction of the gift in 1 Kings 9:11 is not imported into this account.
The text distinguishes forced labor imposed on the remaining peoples from the Israelites’ military and command roles.
The explanation for relocating Pharaoh’s daughter is Solomon’s own statement.
Chronicles gives four hundred fifty talents here; the parallel account in 1 Kings 9:28 gives four hundred twenty.
vocabulary: Mas names an imposed labor levy.
Sukkot recalls dwelling in temporary shelters; it is also called the Festival of Booths.
A large ancient unit of weight, not a coin.

notes: Ascent follows the Hebrew form here; some render it as an offering or the manner in which Solomon offered sacrifice.
The kind of tree called algum is uncertain. Steps renders a term for raised ways; terraces or supports are also proposed.
Beyond what she brought preserves the difficult comparison in Chronicles. It is not replaced with the wording of 1 Kings 10:13.
Shekels supplies the conventional weight unit; the Hebrew gives the numbers without naming that unit.
The last animal name is uncertain; peacocks is traditional, while baboons is another proposed identification.
Iddo is the conventional English name here. The written Hebrew is יעדי; the read form is יֶעְדּוֹ (Yeddo).
vocabulary: The Hebrew says sought Solomon’s face.
A fig-bearing tree, distinct from the tree commonly called sycamore in North America.

notes: Finger is supplied: the Hebrew says my little one. The boast contrasts it with his father’s waist.
Scorpions retains the threatening image. It is often understood as a description of especially cruel whips.
The pinned Hebrew has I will make your yoke heavy, not my father made it heavy. The actual answer differs from the earlier advice.
The narrator attributes the turn of events to God while also describing Rehoboam’s refusal to listen.
vocabulary: A wooden bar used to harness animals; here an image for burdens imposed by the ruler.
The royal family or dynasty, not just a building.

sections.13: Priests and people come to Judah

notes: Goat-demons represents seirim, literally hairy ones or goats, used here for objects of worship.

The read Hebrew has daughter, while the written form has son. The relationship of Abihail to Mahalath is compressed; the draft understands her as Mahalath’s mother, though some take Abihail as a second wife.
The final clause says he sought many wives without specifying for whom. The preceding context concerns his sons.
vocabulary: Migrash refers to the open land associated with a town.
Women in recognized household unions with a status distinct from that of wives.

notes: Some deliverance can also be understood as deliverance soon. The following verse makes clear that subjection to Shishak remains.
Rehoboam’s mother is explicitly identified as an Ammonite.
The Hebrew adds a reference to genealogical registration; its exact connection to the named records is compressed.
vocabulary: Azav is repeated of the people’s action and God’s response.
Avodah can describe worship or labor; here it links serving God and serving foreign rulers.
Royal guards or attendants who accompanied the king.

notes: Micaiah daughter of Uriel is retained as written here. The relationship to the Maacah named in 11:20–22 is not settled by changing the text.
Covenant of salt is an ancient expression for an enduring covenant; the image is retained.
Young and fainthearted belongs to Abijah’s speech. Rehoboam’s stated age at accession in 12:13 is forty-one.
The read form is Ephrain; the written form is Ephron.
The death notice is retained in its narrated position without adjusting the chronology to other regnal notices.
vocabulary: The Hebrew idiom is fill the hand, used for installation in priestly service.
Sha‘an pictures leaning for support; it recurs in Asa’s story.

sections.1: Asa and a time of rest

notes: This verse is numbered 13:23 in the Hebrew source. English verses 14:2–15 correspond to Hebrew 14:1–14.
The first appeal contrasts a great force with powerlessness. It can also be understood as saying that helping the strong or the powerless makes no difference to God.
Could not recover renders an expression that can also mean none remained alive. The main text retains the devastating defeat without resolving it as a precise survivor count.
vocabulary: A person of Cush, associated with the region south of Egypt.
The same leaning-for-support verb is central to Hanani’s rebuke in 16:7–8.

notes: The speech does not name the period it describes.
The Hebrew names Oded here, although verse 1 introduces Azariah son of Oded. The draft retains both notices.
The covenant includes a death penalty for refusal. The following joy does not remove that coercive provision.
The Hebrew calls Maacah Asa’s mother. Mother can include a grandmother or senior female ancestor; 11:20 identifies Maacah as Abijah’s mother.
The remaining high places in Israel are stated alongside the positive judgment of Asa’s heart. Compare the removals in Judah in 14:3–5.
The thirty-fifth year is retained. Together with 16:1, it presents a chronological difficulty beside the regnal dates in 1 Kings.
vocabulary: Nephesh names the living self or life, not only an inner part.
Gebirah is a title for a senior royal woman with recognized authority.

notes: The Hebrew gives the thirty-sixth year of Asa. First Kings 16:8 places Baasha’s successor in Asa’s twenty-sixth year. The draft leaves the discrepancy visible.
The army said to escape is Aram’s, not Israel’s.
The place of imprisonment is literally the house of the stocks.
The criticism concerns Asa’s failure to seek the LORD in this narrative; the verse does not state a general prohibition on physicians.
A great burning in his honor follows the burial description. It need not mean that his body was cremated.
vocabulary: Shalem conveys completeness or undivided commitment.
Darash links inquiry, worship and reliance across these royal stories.

notes: The Hebrew names David and qualifies his ways as earlier.
The lifted-heart expression has a positive sense here, unlike its use for pride in other settings.
Shemiramoth follows the read form of the name.
Extensive work follows the ordinary sense of the Hebrew; some interpret it as supplies or stores in this setting.
vocabulary: Torah includes teaching and direction, not only individual laws.
The verb describes willingly offering oneself.

notes: The court title saris can mean an official or a eunuch.
Micaiah’s first answer sounds like the other prophets’ assurance. The king’s demand for truth introduces the contrasting vision; the Hebrew supplies no explicit tone marker.
The vision describes a lying spirit commissioned before the LORD. It does not identify the spirit by name or explain away the deception.
Scant bread and scant water renders the repeated expression bread/water of distress.
The first clause is compressed; the following action identifies Israel’s king as the one who disguises himself.
The archer acts without knowing the significance of his target. The exact pieces of armor in the wound description are uncertain.
The Hebrew portrays the king keeping himself upright; it does not name an attendant holding him.
vocabulary: A common image for a ruler; the scattered sheep portray a people without one.
Patah can mean persuade or deceive; the ensuing lying spirit makes deception explicit here.
Shalom is the repeated test of the king’s expected safe return.

notes: The Hebrew concludes they returned to Jerusalem. The referent is not specified; some translations instead understand the judges as residing there.
Bloodshed renders the compressed expression between blood and blood, concerning legal distinctions in cases involving death or bloodguilt.
vocabulary: The Hebrew image is lifting faces: treating people according to status rather than justice.
Shoterim are administrative officials; the term does not specify modern police roles.

notes: The pinned Hebrew repeats Ammonites in verse 1 and reads Aram in verse 2. Meunites and Edom are alternative readings often adopted to address these difficulties. Fluent retains the pinned readings.
Who loved you follows the Hebrew participle; your friend is another way to render the relationship.
Sword of judgment represents a difficult compressed phrase; sword, judgment is another division.
Holy splendor can refer to sacred beauty or holy attire. The Hebrew does not specify a garment here.
The ambushers are not identified. The following verse describes the invaders turning on one another.
The Hebrew has corpses in the inventory. Clothing is an alternative reading; the draft preserves the more difficult source word.
The final he can refer to Ahaziah or to Jehoshaphat’s conduct in making the alliance. Fluent follows the nearer named person, Ahaziah.
Chronicles explicitly says the ships were to sail to Tarshish. The different description in 1 Kings 22:48 is not substituted here.
vocabulary: Yeshuah is deliverance; the promised rescue concerns this battle.
Forms of the same Hebrew root, aman, connect reliance with being established.
The name means blessing and echoes they blessed in the same verse.
